inputs.statement: For every interval I=[a,b] in [0,infinity), |I|<=1, and mean-zero continuous piecewise smooth functions f1,f2,f3 with finite Xnorm(I), ||Cop_I(f1,f2,f3)||_2<=C|I| product_j||fj||_X(I)+C||fi||_(L^infinity(I;H^(-pstar))) product_(j!=i)||fj||_(L^infinity(I;L2)) for each i=1,2,3. The same estimate holds for arbitrary continuous functions in Xnorm with L^infinity L2 regularity and a distributional time derivative in L^infinity H^(-pstar). For time-independent mean-zero fj in H^sigma, 0<=sigma<=1, ||Cop_I(f1,f2,f3)||_2<=C_sigma |I|^sigma product_j||fj||_(H^sigma), interpreted with the bounded extension. Constants are uniform in interval location and Fourier support.

For any smooth real mean-zero datum and integer L>=1, tau=T/L, the scheme iterates are smooth, real and mean-zero. With D023 on each step, v^(n+1)=f_n+F_n(t_(n+1))+C_n(t_(n+1))-Remainder_(t_n,tau)(f_n,f_n,f_n). Hence V(t_n)=v^n and V(t_(n+1))=v^(n+1), so V is continuous and piecewise smooth on [0,T]. Also Y_n'=Bop_t(f_n,F_n)+(1/2)Bop_t(F_n,F_n)-W_n/tau, Y_n(t_n)=0, and Rres is continuous, piecewise smooth with Rres'= -Bop_t(Y_n,z_n)-(1/2)Bop_t(Y_n,Y_n)-W_n/tau; consequently V'=(1/2)Bop_t(V,V)+Rres' on each step and distributionally globally. All V,Y_n,z_n,Rres and W_n are mean-zero.

Fix any step n, 0<tau<=1, a mean-zero numerical state f_n in L2 and mean-zero w in H^gamma with ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M0. Define delta_n=||f_n-w||_2<=1 and q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n; use the step formulas D023 with this f_n, initially smooth. Then q_n<=2, ||f_n||_2<=M0+1, sup||F_n||_(H^1)<=C_(M0,gamma), sup||F_n-Stage_n(t;w)||_(H^1)<=C_(M0,gamma)*delta_n, sup||F_n||_(H^agamma)+sup||F_n||_2<=C_(M0,gamma)*q_n, and ||z_n||_X(I_n)<=C_(M0,gamma). Moreover sup||Bop_t(F_n,F_n)||_2<=C_(M0,gamma)*q_n, sup||Q_n||_2+||W_n||_2<=C_(M0,gamma)*tau*q_n, and sup||Dinv Bop_t(f_n,F_n)||_2<=C_(M0,gamma)*q_n. Suprema are over the step; constants are uniform in the step and support.

Under the step hypotheses explicitly stated below, with smooth states initially and the interpolation D023, sup_(I_n)||Dinv Y_n'||_2<=C_(M0,gamma) q_n, sup_(I_n)||Dinv Y_n||_2<=C_(M0,gamma) tau q_n, sup_(I_n)||Y_n||_2<=C_(M0,gamma) q_n, ||Y_n||_X(I_n)<=C_(M0,gamma) q_n and sup_(I_n)||Y_n||_(H^(-pstar))<=C_(M0,gamma) tau q_n. These estimates are uniform in step and Fourier support. Here explicitly the hypotheses are 0<tau<=1, n>=0, mean-zero f_n in L2 and w in H^gamma, ||w||_(H^gamma)<=M0 and delta_n=||f_n-w||_2<=1, q_n=tau^gamma+delta_n.
0<gamma<=1.

output.statement: For smooth real mean-zero initial data, 0<tau=T/L<=1 and an exact twisted solution v with sup||v||_(H^gamma)<=M0, use D023 and suppose delta_n=||v^n-v(t_n)||_2<=1 at a step. Then sup_(I_n)||rho_n||_2<=C_(M0,gamma) tau q_n and ||Rres'||_(L^infinity(I_n;H^(-pstar)))<=C_(M0,gamma) q_n. For any I=[a,b] subset [0,T] starting at a grid point and having h=b-a<=1, define E_I=sup_I||e||_2 for e=v-V. If E_I<=1, then sup_(t in I)||Rres(t)-Rres(a)||_2<=C_(M0,gamma)(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I), ||e||_X(I)<=C_(M0,gamma)(tau^gamma+E_I), and ||v||_X(I)+||V||_X(I)<=C_(M0,gamma). The interval may end inside a step.

locals.declaration: Fix the exact twist v on [0,T] with sup H^gamma norm <=M0.
Fix M0 as the bound on the exact twisted flow.
Fix 0<tau=T/L<=1 with a positive integer L.
Fix the arbitrary step index n with delta_n<=1.
Set w=v(t_n).
Fix I=[a,b] starting at a grid point, with h=b-a<=1 and possibly partial final step.
Set E_I=sup_I||v-V||_2; the extra premise E_I<=1 is L1.

locals.type: real shorthand for the D023 component q_n
locals.declaration: Throughout this unit q_n denotes the defined scalar tau^gamma+delta_n; delta_n is the L2 distance to the chosen comparison state. The tuple components F_n,z_n,C_n,Q_n,W_n,V,Y_n,rho_n,Rres refer exactly to D023.

argument.text: H002 supplies the range 0<gamma<=1 and the guard for agamma. Fix smooth data, an exact twisted flow with H^gamma bound M0, and a step with delta_n<=1. Put w=v(t_n), so N009–N010 apply. In the first integral of rho_n, integrate Bop_t(Y_n,z_n) by N005's normal form, keeping both endpoints. The asymmetric Jop estimate and sup||Dinv Y_n||_2<=C tau q_n bound the endpoint terms by C tau q_n. The term integral Jop_t(Y_n',z_n) is <=tau*C q_n by the Dinv Y_n' bound and ||z_n||_2<=C. Since z_n'=(1/2)Bop_t(f_n,f_n), the other term is (1/2)Cop(f_n,f_n,Y_n). Apply N006 with the negative norm on Y_n: its first term is <=C tau q_n because f_n is constant with bounded Xnorm and ||Y_n||_X<=C q_n; its second term is <=C tau q_n by the small H^(-pstar) norm of Y_n. Thus the first integral of rho_n is <=C tau q_n, uniformly at every partial-step endpoint.

produces.statement: For every partial endpoint of the step, ||integral Bop_t(Y_n,z_n)dt||_2<=C tau q_n.

argument.text: For integral Bop_t(Y_n,Y_n), the same normal form gives endpoint terms <=C tau q_n^2 and derivative terms <=tau*C q_n^2 using the asymmetric Jop estimate, Dinv Y_n and Dinv Y_n', and ||Y_n||_2<=C q_n. Since q_n<=2 this is <=C tau q_n. The affine W_n term is <=||W_n||_2<=C tau q_n by N009. Thus sup||rho_n||_2<=C tau q_n. By N008, Rres'=-Bop_t(Y_n,z_n)-(1/2)Bop_t(Y_n,Y_n)-W_n/tau; N005's Bop negative-norm bound, N009–N010 and q_n<=2 give ||Rres'||_(L^infinity H^(-pstar))<=C q_n.

produces.statement: On a step with delta_n<=1, sup||rho_n||_2<=C tau q_n and ||Rres'||_(L^infinity H^(-pstar))<=C q_n.

argument.text: Now fix any interval I=[a,b] starting at a grid point, h<=1, and temporarily assume L1: E_I=sup_I||e||_2<=1. There are at most h/tau+1 intersected steps, each beginning within I, with delta_n=||e(t_n)||_2<=E_I because N008 gives V(t_n)=v^n. Sum F002 over complete steps and the final partial step to obtain sup||Rres(t)-Rres(a)||_2<=C(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I). Differentiating the exact twist gives v'=(1/2)Bop_t(v,v); subtract N008 to obtain e'=Bop_t(e,v-e/2)-Rres'. N005 bounds its negative norm by C E_I+C(tau^gamma+E_I), proving ||e||_X<=C(tau^gamma+E_I). The exact L2 bound gives ||v||_X<=C; then V=v-e gives ||V||_X<=C, since tau^gamma<=1 and E_I<=1. Discharge L1, retain its antecedent, and quantify over all intervals and flows.

Since v'=(1/2)Bop(v,v), e'=Bop(e,g)-Rres' and g'=(1/2)Bop(v,v)-(1/2)Bop(e,g)+(1/2)Rres', symmetry of Jop and its Bop-to-Cop identity yield exactly F_I(t)=(1/3)[Jop_s(e,g)]_a^t-(1/3)Cop_[a,t](e,g,V)-(1/6)Cop_[a,t](v,v,e)+(1/3)integral_a^t Jop_s(Rres',V)ds. After P_gt(N), both endpoints are <=C N^(-1) E_I by the H^1 Jop estimate, including the endpoint at a even when e(a)!=0. Apply the identity stepwise and telescope internal endpoints when necessary.

argument.text: For any three permitted inputs, put Low=P_leq(N/3) and High equal to its complementary Fourier projection. The expression Cop(f1,f2,f3)-Cop(Low f1,Low f2,Low f3) equals Cop(High f1,f2,f3)+Cop(Low f1,High f2,f3)+Cop(Low f1,Low f2,High f3). The all-low output has no frequencies above N, since each Fourier product has sum of its input frequencies and neither the group nor inverse derivative changes support. Projections contract Xnorm. For each designated high input, ||High fj||_(H^(-pstar))<=C N^(-pstar)||fj||_2 by its Fourier support. N006 with the negative norm on that slot therefore gives ||P_gt(N)Cop_[a,t](f1,f2,f3)||_2<=C h product||fj||_X(I)+C N^(-pstar) product||fj||_(L^infinity(I;L2)). For the two cubic terms of F002, N011 bounds the Xnorm of e by C(tau^gamma+E_I), all other Xnorms by C, and their L2 products by C E_I. Thus these terms total <=C h tau^gamma+C(h+N^(-pstar))E_I.

produces.statement: Under L1 the two high-output cubic terms in the normal-form formula total at most C h tau^gamma+C(h+N^(-pstar))E_I.

argument.text: It remains to bound the forcing integral in F002 using the actual residual. On each intersected step N008 rewrites Jop_s(Rres',V) as -Jop_s(Bop_s(Y_n,z_n),V)-(1/2)Jop_s(Bop_s(Y_n,Y_n),V)-tau^(-1)Jop_s(W_n,V). The W_n integral is <=tau^(-1)*tau*C||W_n||_2 sup||V||_2<=C tau q_n by N005 and N009. Every intersected step starts inside I, so q_n<=tau^gamma+E_I; there are <=h/tau+1 such steps. Summing gives C(h+tau)(tau^gamma+E_I), also for a partial final step.

argument.text: Combine F002–F004 to get sup||P_gt(N)F_I||_2<=C(h+tau)tau^gamma+C(h+tau+N^(-1)+N^(-pstar))E_I. Use F001 and N011's bound on Rres(t)-Rres(a) in the error identity. definitions.definition: Ttor = reals/(2*pi*integers), with normalized measure dx/(2*pi); spatial products and integrals are on this domain.
For an integrable periodic f, Fourier(f)(k)=hat f(k)=(2*pi)^(-1) integral_0^(2*pi) f(x) exp(-i*k*x) dx; the transform extends to distributions by duality.

For every real s, H^s(Ttor) is the completion of trigonometric polynomials with ||f||_(H^s)^2=sum_(k in Z) <k>^(2*s)|hat f(k)|^2, <k>=(1+k^2)^(1/2). Negative spaces are interpreted as distributions. Homogeneous norms on zero-mean distributions are ||f||_(dot H^s)^2=sum_(k!=0)|k|^(2*s)|hat f(k)|^2. Real means hat f(-k)=conjugate(hat f(k)); mean zero means hat f(0)=0.

L2=H^0(Ttor), with ||f||_2^2=(2*pi)^(-1) integral |f|^2 dx. More generally L^p uses the same normalized measure; L^infinity is essential supremum. 647: 5 Numerical experiments
648: The numerical library implements the displayed update with Fourier coefficients on−K,...,K .
649: Polynomial products are full linear convolutions. The quadratic stage has support through2K;
650: cubic terms retain support through3K. Only the completed step is projected to|k|≤K . ThusK

651: is a fixed spatial approximation parameter, independent ofτ. These finite computations are distinct
652: from the time-semidiscrete theorem. The routines use direct convolution for short arrays and padded
653: FFT convolution for longer arrays, with no circular aliasing in either path. A step costsO(KlogK )
654: with FFT products andO(K)working storage; retaining allL + 1states costs O(LK). The direct
655: triple sum forR2 costs O(N 3)time and working storage in the present verification implementation.

ON THE REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC
KORTEWEG–DE VRIES EQUATION
Anatoli V. Babin 1, Alexei A. Ilyin 2 and Edriss S. Titi 3
This paper is dedicated to the memory of Professor Basil Nicolaenko
Abstract. In this paper we develop and use successive averaging method s for explaining the regular-
ization mechanism in the the periodic Korteweg–de Vries (Kd V) equation in the homogeneous Sobolev
spaces ˙H s, for s ≥ 0. Speciﬁcally, we prove the global existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuous
dependence on the initial data of the solutions of the period ic KdV. For the case where the initial data
is in L2 we also show the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these so lutions with respect to the initial
data as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s, for s ∈ (−1, 0].
Keywords: Korteweg–de Vries equation, dispersive equations, averaging met hod, non-
linear resonance.
MSC: 35B34,35Q53.
1. Introduction
This paper is motivated by works on global regularity of solutions of 3 D problems in
hydrodynamics (Navier-Stokes or Boussinesq system with periodic boundary conditions)
in the presence of fast rotation or strong stratiﬁcation, see, e.g ., [1], [2], [3], [4], [11],
[12], [18], [16], [20], [26], and references therein. The results are base d on the presence of
high-frequency waves that lead to destructive interference and eﬀectively weaken the non-
linearity through time averaging allowing to prove global regularity of solutions for these
problems, at the limit of inﬁnite rotation. The above mentioned hydro dynamical problems
are rather complicated (Boussinesq system, for example, involves ﬁve unknown functions of
three spatial variables and time, the equations are coupled throug h a quadratic nonlinear-
ity). Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to apply this averagin g approach to a slightly
simpler problem to make these ideas more transparent. Here we con sider the Korteweg–de
Vries equation with one spatial variable subjected to periodic bound ary condition. The
averaging eﬀects are strong because on high Fourier modes the line ar term generates high-
frequency oscillations which weakens the nonlinearity and makes it mild er. In this paper
we show connections between the smoothness properties of solut ions of the Korteweg–de
Vries (KdV) equation and the algebraic structure of the nonlinear r esonances between the
high-frequency oscillations. Our main goal is to make the relations be tween time-averaging
eﬀects and smoothness issues more explicit, rather than to obtain global regularity results
under minimal restrictions (see, e.g., [5], [7], [14] and the references therein). In particular,
our approach and aim are completely diﬀerent than the machinery an d harmonic analysis

tools that were developed over the past decade and half for invest igating dispersive partial
diﬀerential equations (see the discussion and references mention ed below). Moreover, we
also remark that the tools and ideas that are developed in this contr ibution can be easily
applied to multi-dimensional equations and multi-component systems , a subject of future
investigation.
It is worth mentioning that similar approach, taking advantage of tim e averaging, has
also been applied to the two-dimensional rotating inviscid Burgers eq uations in [1] and
[16] to show that fast rotation prevents the formation of a ﬁnite t ime singularity in the
two-dimensional Burgers system. We will use this warmup toy model, and in particular
the approach in [1], to ﬁx ideas and to illustrate in section 2 the averag ing mechanism,
which is instrumental in regularizing the solutions and in preventing th e formation of a
ﬁnite time singularity for the two-dimensional inviscid Burgers syste m.
Our approach consists of three steps. First, we rewrite the prob lem as a system of
ODE for time-dependent Fourier coeﬃcients. This is a standard app roach to the periodic
problem which is commonly used. Second, to make the eﬀects of time a veraging explicit
we single out oscillating factors and do several integration by parts , with respect to time,
to obtain several generations of equations for slowly varying coeﬃ cients. Resonances
reveal themselves as obstacles to the integrations by parts and p roduce resonant terms
in the equations, integrated terms become more and more regular. Higher generations of
equations allow solutions with less regularity. This algorithm is simple and straightforward,
it does not use ﬁne methods such as analytic reduction to linear form s and analysis of self
similar solutions or the construction of conserved or almost conser ved quantities. The third
step is analysis of the obtained equations. To show their regularity w e use straightforward
estimates of multilinear operators, energy estimates and the Cont raction principle. To use
the contraction principle in negative Sobolev spaces we use splitting t o high and low Fourier
modes and exploit averaging-induced squeezing of higher modes. In order to justify our
estimates we use a Galerkin approximations procedure. We try to us e methods which can
be easily adjusted to general multidimensional problems such as tho se mentioned above
in hydrodynamic problems. We do not use in our analysis the speciﬁc pr operties of the
KdV equation such as complete integrability or special conserved qu antities. Moreover,
one can expect that in order to obtain more delicate information one has to resort to the
use of higher generations of equations, i.e. more integrations by pa rt.
The paper is organized as follows. In section 3 we reformulate the Kd V equation in
terms of its Fourier components and introduce the notion of weak s olution; we also make
two types of formal transformations of the equation which will be u sed for proving the
relevant well-posedness results. In section 4 we use the Galerkin pr ocedure for proving the
global existence in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s >0. In section 5 we use the Contraction
Principle to show that the solutions established in section 4 are unique and Lipschitz
continuous, with respect to the initial data, in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s ≥ 1/2. A
more technical section 6 is devoted to proving similar results for s ∈ [0, 1/2], where the
case s = 0 is dealt with separately. Finally, for solutions with initial data in L2 we show
the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions, with resp ect to the initial data,
as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s for all s ∈ (−1, 0].
There is a long history of the KdV equations in the periodical setting. We do not attempt
to give here a complete survey of this long history, but we are satisﬁ ed by mentioning,
below, some of the key landmark results. First Bourgain [6] proved local well-posedness in
L2. We observe that the result of Bourgain also implies global existence for the real valued
KdV in L2. Later the local well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s > −1/2, was

REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION 3
established for the real and complex valued KdV by Kenig, Ponce, an d Vega [14]. Later
global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1/2, was established for the real
valued KdV by Colliander, Keel, Staﬃlani, Takaoka and Tao [7]. Using th e fact that the
KdV equation is an integrable system, and by implementing the inverse method, Kappeler
and Topalov [15] proved global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1.
Even though the results presented in this contribution are weaker than the state-of-the-
art results mentioned above, our approach is substantially diﬀeren t and easy to master.
Speciﬁcally, and as we have stressed above, our approach is based on systematic applica-
tion of time averaging. It is worth mentioning that since we rewrite th e KdV equation
in diﬀerent forms, based on the diﬀerentiation by parts with respec t to the time variable,
there is superﬁcial similarity with the reduction to normal forms (cf . [19]). The diﬀerence
is that the consecutive forms of the KdV, which we derive, are base d not on the geometric
properties such as a reduction to a linear form or a reduction to inva riant tori, but ex-
clusively on time averaging properties. In order to stress the eﬀec ts, which are due solely
to the time averaging, we do not use energy conservation or modiﬁe d energy functionals
as in the I-method. We use only the L2 norm conservation to mimic the situation which
occurs in the three-dimensional Euler equations and other hydrod ynamical systems.
Moreover, we believe that the averaging approach presented her e can be pushed further
to achieve the best known results concerning the KdV equation. Fu rthermore, diﬀerent
nonlinear dispersive and wave equations, such as the m-KdV, the Kle in-Gordon equation
and water wave equations (see for example, [13], [19], [23]-[25], and re ferences therein),
can possibly be studied quite similarly, a subject of future research .
2. The Complex Burgers equation with fast rotation — a paradigm for
the averaging mechanism
In this section we consider the complex Burgers equation with fast r otation as a warmup
toy model to demonstrate the averaging mechanism for preventin g the formation of sin-
gularity.
The one-dimensional Burgers equation

equation:

equation, the solution develops a ﬁnite time singularity if the initial dat a,ϕ, maps R into

original_context.full_target:
The complete Theorem 1 (Logarithm-free convergence), with its Section 2 standing definitions and fixed scheme, on PDF page 2.

Use the periodic domain mathbbT = reals/(2*pi*integers) with normalized measure dx/(2*pi). For a periodic function f, hat f(k) = (2*pi)^(-1) integral_0^(2*pi) f(x) exp(-i*k*x) dx and <k> = (1+k^2)^(1/2). The Sobolev norm is ||f||_(H^s)^2 = sum_(k in Z) <k>^(2*s) |hat f(k)|^2. These spaces are completions of trigonometric polynomials in these norms, with negative-order spaces interpreted as distributions. Reality means hat f(-k) = conjugate(hat f(k)); mean zero means hat f(0) = 0. Time suprema use continuous representatives; derivative norms use essential suprema.

Let S_t = exp(-t*partial_x^3), with Fourier multiplier exp(i*t*k^3). Let P0 be the spatial mean and P = I-P0. Let D^(-1) = partial_x^(-1) have multiplier (i*k)^(-1) for k != 0 and zero at k=0, and D^(-2) = (D^(-1))^2. The equation is
  u_t + u_xxx = (1/2)*partial_x(u^2), u(0)=u0.
The exact solution is the unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) distributional solution obtained by smooth approximation.

For timestep tau=T/L, the time-semidiscrete scheme is exactly
  u^0 = u0,
  u^(n+1) = S_tau u^n + F_tau(u^n) + H_tau(u^n),
where all products below are spatial products and [G(s)]_(s=0)^(s=tau) means G(tau)-G(0):
  F_tau(f) = (1/6)*P[(S_tau D^(-1) f)^2]
             - (1/6)*S_tau P[(D^(-1) f)^2],
  H_tau(f) = (1/3)*P[(S_tau D^(-1) f)*D^(-1) F_tau(f)]
             + (tau/9)*(S_tau D^(-1) f)*P0(f^2)
             - (1/54)*[S_(tau-s) D^(-1)[(S_s D^(-1) f)^3]]_(s=0)^(s=tau)
             - (1/(27*tau))*[S_(tau-s) D^(-2)[(S_(s-tau) D^(-2) F_tau(f))*(S_s D^(-1) f)]]_(s=0)^(s=tau).
This is the source scheme (2), with no spatial frequency cutoff.

For every T>0, 0<gamma<=1 and R>0, there exist C>0 and tau0>0 depending only on T,gamma,R such that, for every real mean-zero u0 in H^gamma(mathbbT) with ||u0||_(H^gamma)<=R and every positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau0, this fixed scheme satisfies
  max_(0<=n<=L) ||u(n*tau)-u^n||_(L^2) <= C*tau^gamma.
The constants are uniform over the entire stated initial-data ball and all permitted timesteps, with no Fourier-support restriction. The target includes all the hypotheses, quantifiers, endpoints, solution convention and method above.

original_context.full_target:
The complete Theorem 1 (Logarithm-free convergence), with its Section 2 standing definitions and fixed scheme, on PDF page 2.

Use the periodic domain mathbbT = reals/(2*pi*integers) with normalized measure dx/(2*pi). For a periodic function f, hat f(k) = (2*pi)^(-1) integral_0^(2*pi) f(x) exp(-i*k*x) dx and <k> = (1+k^2)^(1/2). The Sobolev norm is ||f||_(H^s)^2 = sum_(k in Z) <k>^(2*s) |hat f(k)|^2. These spaces are completions of trigonometric polynomials in these norms, with negative-order spaces interpreted as distributions. Reality means hat f(-k) = conjugate(hat f(k)); mean zero means hat f(0) = 0. Time suprema use continuous representatives; derivative norms use essential suprema.

Let S_t = exp(-t*partial_x^3), with Fourier multiplier exp(i*t*k^3). Let P0 be the spatial mean and P = I-P0. Let D^(-1) = partial_x^(-1) have multiplier (i*k)^(-1) for k != 0 and zero at k=0, and D^(-2) = (D^(-1))^2. The equation is
  u_t + u_xxx = (1/2)*partial_x(u^2), u(0)=u0.
The exact solution is the unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) distributional solution obtained by smooth approximation.

For timestep tau=T/L, the time-semidiscrete scheme is exactly
  u^0 = u0,
  u^(n+1) = S_tau u^n + F_tau(u^n) + H_tau(u^n),
where all products below are spatial products and [G(s)]_(s=0)^(s=tau) means G(tau)-G(0):
  F_tau(f) = (1/6)*P[(S_tau D^(-1) f)^2]
             - (1/6)*S_tau P[(D^(-1) f)^2],
  H_tau(f) = (1/3)*P[(S_tau D^(-1) f)*D^(-1) F_tau(f)]
             + (tau/9)*(S_tau D^(-1) f)*P0(f^2)
             - (1/54)*[S_(tau-s) D^(-1)[(S_s D^(-1) f)^3]]_(s=0)^(s=tau)
             - (1/(27*tau))*[S_(tau-s) D^(-2)[(S_(s-tau) D^(-2) F_tau(f))*(S_s D^(-1) f)]]_(s=0)^(s=tau).
This is the source scheme (2), with no spatial frequency cutoff.

For every T>0, 0<gamma<=1 and R>0, there exist C>0 and tau0>0 depending only on T,gamma,R such that, for every real mean-zero u0 in H^gamma(mathbbT) with ||u0||_(H^gamma)<=R and every positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau0, this fixed scheme satisfies
  max_(0<=n<=L) ||u(n*tau)-u^n||_(L^2) <= C*tau^gamma.
The constants are uniform over the entire stated initial-data ball and all permitted timesteps, with no Fourier-support restriction. The target includes all the hypotheses, quantifiers, endpoints, solution convention and method above.
original_context.conclusion: There exist positive constants C and tau0 depending only on T,gamma,R such that, for every real mean-zero u0 in H^gamma(Ttor) with ||u0||_(H^gamma)<=R and every positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau0, the exact KdV solution in D012 exists and the unmodified unfiltered scheme D009–D011 is well defined and satisfies max_(0<=n<=L)||u(n*tau)-u^n||_(L2)<=C*tau^gamma. These constants are uniform on the entire initial-data ball, all permitted timesteps, and all Fourier supports, with the domain, normalized measure, Fourier/Sobolev conventions, Airy group, projections, inverse derivatives and full Ftau,Htau formula fixed in D001–D012.

  u_t + u_xxx = (1/2)*partial_x(u^2), u(0)=u0.
The exact solution is the unique real mean-zero C([0,T];H^gamma) distributional solution obtained by smooth approximation.

For timestep tau=T/L, the time-semidiscrete scheme is exactly
  u^0 = u0,
  u^(n+1) = S_tau u^n + F_tau(u^n) + H_tau(u^n),
where all products below are spatial products and [G(s)]_(s=0)^(s=tau) means G(tau)-G(0):
  F_tau(f) = (1/6)*P[(S_tau D^(-1) f)^2]
             - (1/6)*S_tau P[(D^(-1) f)^2],
  H_tau(f) = (1/3)*P[(S_tau D^(-1) f)*D^(-1) F_tau(f)]
             + (tau/9)*(S_tau D^(-1) f)*P0(f^2)
             - (1/54)*[S_(tau-s) D^(-1)[(S_s D^(-1) f)^3]]_(s=0)^(s=tau)
             - (1/(27*tau))*[S_(tau-s) D^(-2)[(S_(s-tau) D^(-2) F_tau(f))*(S_s D^(-1) f)]]_(s=0)^(s=tau).
This is the source scheme (2), with no spatial frequency cutoff.

For every T>0, 0<gamma<=1 and R>0, there exist C>0 and tau0>0 depending only on T,gamma,R such that, for every real mean-zero u0 in H^gamma(mathbbT) with ||u0||_(H^gamma)<=R and every positive integer L with tau=T/L<=tau0, this fixed scheme satisfies
  max_(0<=n<=L) ||u(n*tau)-u^n||_(L^2) <= C*tau^gamma.
The constants are uniform over the entire stated initial-data ball and all permitted timesteps, with no Fourier-support restriction. The target includes all the hypotheses, quantifiers, endpoints, solution convention and method above.
